## 🎯 The task

You have a series. Today you look at it properly, commit to a claim about it, and then
find out what the claim was worth.

The claim: of the four simple methods from Week 1 — mean, naive, drift, seasonal naive —
**which will be hardest to beat on your series?** You answer from the graphics, before you
run anything. Then you run all four and see.

## 📐 Section 1 — Data preparation (1 point)

Load your series and put it on a regular time grid.

- Resolve duplicated timestamps if there are any, and say in one sentence what you decided
  and why.
- Fill the calendar so gaps become visible missing values rather than absent rows.
- State the frequency, the span, and how many complete seasonal cycles you have.

You did all of this in Week 1. It should take ten minutes.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## ⚠️ If your series ends with missing values

Some series in the pool stop being reported years before their last row: the file ends
with a long run of blanks. `interpolate()` will happily fill those by repeating the last
value, and then your holdout is a flat line you invented — every method "predicts" it
perfectly and the exercise is meaningless.

**Trim to the last real observation** before you split, and say in your report that you did
and how much you dropped. Filling interior gaps is repair; filling the tail is fabrication.
:::


::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## ⚠️ Where this goes wrong: the frequency string

- `"W"` does not mean "weekly". It means *week ending Sunday*. If your timestamps are
  Mondays, a grid built with `"W"` lines up with nothing and your series comes back empty.
  Use the anchored form, `"W-MON"` — which is what `spec["freq"]` already gives you.
- pandas 3 removed the bare `"M"`, `"Q"`, `"Y"` and `"H"` aliases. Use `"MS"`/`"ME"`,
  `"QS"`/`"QE"`, `"YS"`/`"YE"` and lowercase `"h"`. A bare `"Q"` now raises rather than warns.
- `"MS"` is month **start**, `"ME"` is month **end**. Pick the one your timestamps already
  use, or every row misses the grid by a few days.

After building a grid, check you did not lose everything: `s["y"].notna().sum()` should be
close to the number of rows you started with.

📖 [offset aliases](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/timeseries.html#offset-aliases) ·
[anchored offsets](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/timeseries.html#anchored-offsets) ·
[`date_range`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.date_range.html) ·
[`reindex`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.reindex.html) ·
[`duplicated`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.duplicated.html)
:::

## 📊 Section 2 — EDA and visualisation (4 points)

Four plots, each with a sentence saying what you see. A plot with no reading attached earns
nothing.

**Graphics.** Time plot, seasonal plot, seasonal subseries plot, ACF. Name the patterns:
trend, seasonality, cycles, level shifts, outliers. Say whether the seasonal swing grows
with the level of the series — you will need that observation next week.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## ⚠️ Where this goes wrong

- `plot_acf` raises once `lags` reaches the length of the series. `lags=min(40, len(y) // 3)`
  is a safe default; for weekly data use at least 60 so the annual spike is visible.
- Plot the ACF with missing values removed — `plot_acf` will not handle `NaN` for you.

📖 [`plot_acf`](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots.plot_acf.html)
:::

**Then commit.** Which of the four methods will be hardest to beat, and why? Write three or
four sentences citing what is *in the plots* — the size of the seasonal swing against the
size of the trend, whether the pattern repeats in the same shape, whether the level moved
recently.

::: {.callout-important}
Write this **before** you run Section 3. The point is not the guess; it is whether you can
read a series. A well-argued wrong prediction earns full marks — an unargued right one
earns nothing.
:::

## 🔢 Section 3 — Implementation (2 points)

**The four methods.** Implement them yourself — they are four lines each, and they are on
the [Week 1 slides](https://01a05924-a704-8747-1dda-9917ad1a3d63.share.connect.posit.cloud) if you need them.

$$
\hat{y}_{T+h} = \bar{y}
\qquad
\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_T
\qquad
\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_{T+h-m}
\qquad
\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_T + h\,\frac{y_T - y_1}{T-1}
$$

**The holdout.** Cut off the last full seasonal cycle — one year of data — fit nothing, and
forecast that span with all four. Report the RMSE of each, and the ratio of each to the
best. That ratio is the skill score from the lecture: it says how much worse a method is
than the bar.

**The verdict.** Which won? Did your prediction hold? If it did not, say what in the plots
you misread — that sentence is worth more than the prediction was.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## ⚠️ Where this goes wrong

- `snaive` needs the last `m` observations of the **training** part, not of the whole
  series. If your forecast looks suspiciously perfect, you are forecasting with the answer.
- Drop or interpolate missing values before scoring: an `NaN` anywhere in the holdout makes
  every RMSE `NaN`.
- RMSE is in the units of your series, so it is only comparable *between methods on the same
  series* — never between your series and a classmate's. That is what the ratio is for.
:::
